reading.body:
AI risk is being repriced and moved out of standard insurance into captives, mutual pools, surplus lines, and capital markets, with coverage tied directly to compute availability and model performance.

The pattern is substitution. Where traditional carriers decline risk, hyperscalers form single parent captives to self-insure, startups pool catastrophic legal costs, and complex AI liability migrates to surplus lines and Lloyds. Parametric micro-insurance pays out on API and GPU availability, and catastrophe bonds hedge multi-day cloud outages, so compute uptime becomes an insurable event rather than an assumed operating condition.

For AI specifically, this means insurance is starting to track the two things that determine whether models can run at all: compute access and output reliability. Insured performance guarantees back vendor commitments on model output, while certification-linked discounts reward enterprises that pass third party safety audits. Generative AI exclusion endorsements remove that risk from general liability cover, and reinsurance capacity caps limit the maximum cover available to operators.

What the data does not show is scale or price. It lists ten mechanisms but gives no premiums, loss ratios, claim volumes, or binding capacity figures. It also says nothing about physical power or building risk, which are not among these instruments.

The ten mechanisms split into two groups that do different jobs. Six of them move risk off the standard balance sheet: captives, mutual pools, surplus lines, exclusions, capacity caps, and reinsurance limits. Four of them create new instruments where no standard market exists: parametric micro-insurance, catastrophe bonds, insured performance guarantees, and certification discounts. The first group is defensive, a retreat by carriers. The second is constructive, a new market pricing things that were previously unpriceable.

The constructive group prices two underlying variables, and they are the same two the rest of the stack depends on. Parametric policies trigger on API and GPU availability. Catastrophe bonds trigger on multi-day cloud shutdowns. Insured performance guarantees trigger on model output. So the insurance layer is writing contracts against compute access and output reliability, which means the cost of insuring an AI business now moves with the same variables as the cost of running one.

The defensive group has a ceiling built into it. Reinsurance capacity caps set the maximum cover available, and generative AI exclusion endorsements remove the risk from general liability entirely. An operator that cannot buy cover in the standard market and cannot buy enough in the specialty market has one remaining option, which is to hold the risk itself. That is what the captives and mutual pools are for, and it is why they appear alongside the exclusions rather than instead of them.

What does a hyperscaler single parent captive actually insure?
It carries risk that commercial carriers decline, according to the data. The data does not name which risks, which hyperscalers, or any captive's size.

How does parametric micro-insurance decide when to pay out?
Payouts are triggered by API and GPU cloud availability. The policies are small and instant, aimed at developers rather than enterprises.

Can catastrophe bonds cover an AI company's losses from a cloud outage?
They hedge financial exposure to multi-day cloud shutdowns, so the trigger is the duration of the outage rather than a specific company's loss. The data gives no issuance size, pricing, or which clouds are covered.

What do generative AI exclusion endorsements exclude, exactly?
They are standardised wording that removes generative AI risk from general liability cover. The data does not reproduce the wording or say which carriers adopt it.

Do certification-linked discounts require a specific audit?
They are discount programmes for enterprises that pass a third party safety audit. The data does not name the auditor, the standard, or the size of the discount.

Is there any figure for premiums, claims, or capacity in this data?
No. The data lists ten mechanisms with one-line descriptions and no premiums, loss ratios, claim volumes, or binding capacity numbers. It also contains nothing on physical power or building risk.
